title: SUPPLEMENTARY — rz-tools 2D Formulation and Discretization Explorer by the same lecturer (heat conduction · Galerkin · Q4 Lagrange FEM)
context: Secondary material by the same lecturer, from his rz-tools. It writes every pairing in one notation (indices I, J; {Q} + {B} = {R}; a parameter square with a Jacobian). Where it writes something differently from the course page, follow the course page; use this only for explanations the course page lacks, in the course page's notation.

blocks.text:
[tool-form2d-s1] rz-tools form2d (heat conduction · Galerkin · Q4 Lagrange FEM) · 1 · Governing equation and boundary conditions
The unknown is the temperature T(x,y). From the energy balance of a differential element with Fourier's law, steady heat conduction with heat generation q_h is governed by

\dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}\!\left(k_x\frac{\partial T}{\partial x}\right) + \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}\!\left(k_y\frac{\partial T}{\partial y}\right) = -q_h \qquad \text{in}\ \Omega

It is convenient to write this with the differential operator vector \{\partial\} and the conductivity matrix [E]; here the material is isotropic, k_x = k_y = k = 1, and q_h = 0:

\{\partial\}[E]\{\partial\}^T T = -q_h, \qquad \{\partial\} = \begin{Bmatrix}\dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} & \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}\end{Bmatrix}, \qquad [E] = \begin{bmatrix} k_x & 0\\ 0 & k_y\end{bmatrix} = k\begin{bmatrix}1 & 0\\ 0 & 1\end{bmatrix}

The PDE must be supplemented by boundary condition equations. On \Gamma_N the natural (Neumann) condition prescribes the flux or the traction; on \Gamma_D the essential (Dirichlet) condition prescribes the unknown itself. Every edge of the patch is one or the other, \Gamma_D \cup \Gamma_N = \Gamma:

\left(k_x\frac{\partial T}{\partial x}\right)\!\Big|_b\, n_x + \left(k_y\frac{\partial T}{\partial y}\right)\!\Big|_b\, n_y = q_b \quad \text{on}\ \Gamma_N, \qquad T\big|_b = \bar T \quad \text{on}\ \Gamma_D
Boundary of this model
\xi = 0	\Gamma_N	natural, loaded	q_b = 1 (flux into the domain)
\xi = 1	\Gamma_D	essential (Dirichlet)	T = \bar T = 1
\eta = 0	\Gamma_N	natural, zero	q_b = 0 (insulated)
\eta = 1	\Gamma_N	natural, zero	q_b = 0 (insulated)

Change the edges in the control panel and watch which terms survive in the following steps.

blocks.text:
[tool-form2d-s2] rz-tools form2d (heat conduction · Galerkin · Q4 Lagrange FEM) · 2 · From the PDE to an integral statement
Inserting an approximation T^h with n unknowns into the PDE does not satisfy it pointwise; the residual is made to vanish in a weighted-integral sense instead. To obtain n independent equations, the residual is multiplied by each weight function w_I in turn and integrated over the domain (weighted residual method):

\int_\Omega w_I\left[\dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}\!\left(k\frac{\partial T^h}{\partial x}\right) + \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}\!\left(k\frac{\partial T^h}{\partial y}\right) + q_h\right]d\Omega = 0, \qquad I = 1,\dots,n

Integration by parts (the divergence theorem applied to the product w_I\,k\,\partial T^h/\partial x, and likewise in y) relaxes the continuity requirement, one derivative moving from T^h to w_I, and induces the natural boundary terms explicitly:

-\int_\Omega\left(k\frac{\partial w_I}{\partial x}\frac{\partial T^h}{\partial x} + k\frac{\partial w_I}{\partial y}\frac{\partial T^h}{\partial y}\right)d\Omega + \oint_\Gamma w_I\left(k\frac{\partial T^h}{\partial x}n_x + k\frac{\partial T^h}{\partial y}n_y\right)d\Gamma + \int_\Omega w_I\,q_h\,d\Omega = 0

On \Gamma_D the weight function is taken as zero (the value is known there), and on \Gamma_N the flux is the prescribed q_b. Rearranging gives the weak form:

\int_\Omega\left(k\frac{\partial w_I}{\partial x}\frac{\partial T^h}{\partial x} + k\frac{\partial w_I}{\partial y}\frac{\partial T^h}{\partial y}\right)d\Omega = \int_\Omega w_I\,q_h\,d\Omega + \int_{\Gamma_N} w_I\,q_b\,d\Gamma, \qquad I = 1,\dots,n

Both w_I and T^h now carry first derivatives only, so C^0 shape functions suffice. The natural condition has entered by itself through the boundary integral; the essential condition has to be imposed on the discretized system (step 6).

blocks.text:
[tool-form2d-s5] rz-tools form2d (heat conduction · Galerkin · Q4 Lagrange FEM) · 5 · Discretization: the component equations
Inserting the approximation into the weak form with w_I = N_I, and taking the unknowns (constants) outside the integrals, gives one equation for each I:

\sum_{J=1}^{n}\left[\int_\Omega\left(k\frac{\partial N_I}{\partial x}\frac{\partial N_J}{\partial x} + k\frac{\partial N_I}{\partial y}\frac{\partial N_J}{\partial y}\right)d\Omega\right]\hat T_J = \int_\Omega N_I\,q_h\,d\Omega + \int_{\Gamma_N} N_I\,q_b\,d\Gamma, \qquad I = 1,\dots,n

Now let us define the following matrix and vectors. The integral on the left is the conductance matrix, the integrals on the right the heat-generation vector and the natural boundary condition vector:

[K] = \int_\Omega \{N\}^T\{\partial\}[E]\{\partial\}^T\{N\}\,d\Omega, \qquad \{Q\} = \int_\Omega \{N\}^T q_h\,d\Omega, \qquad \{B\} = \int_{\Gamma_N}\{N\}^T q_b\,d\Gamma

A typical entry, for example K_{34}, is obtained by carrying the multiplication from left to right and integrating:

K_{34} = \int_\Omega\left(k_x\frac{\partial N_3}{\partial x}\frac{\partial N_4}{\partial x} + k_y\frac{\partial N_3}{\partial y}\frac{\partial N_4}{\partial y}\right)d\Omega, \qquad Q_3 = \int_\Omega N_3\,q_h\,d\Omega, \qquad B_3 = \int_{\Gamma_N} N_3\,q_b\,d\Gamma

The integrals are evaluated cell by cell: \Omega is the union of n_e = 16 cells \Omega_e (elements), each the image of a parameter cell \widehat\Omega_e, which in turn is the image of the parent square. With the derivative transformation of step 4 and Gauss quadrature, n_g\times n_g = 2\times2 points per cell,

K_{IJ} = \sum_{e=1}^{n_e}\int_{\widehat\Omega_e}\left(k\frac{\partial N_I}{\partial x}\frac{\partial N_J}{\partial x} + k\frac{\partial N_I}{\partial y}\frac{\partial N_J}{\partial y}\right)|\det[J]|\,d\xi\,d\eta
\approx \sum_{e=1}^{n_e}\sum_{g=1}^{4}\left(k\frac{\partial N_I}{\partial x}\frac{\partial N_J}{\partial x} + k\frac{\partial N_I}{\partial y}\frac{\partial N_J}{\partial y}\right)_{\!g}|\det[J]|_g\,\frac{\Delta\xi_e\,\Delta\eta_e}{4}\,W_g

where W_g is the product of the two 1D Gauss weights and \Delta\xi_e\,\Delta\eta_e/4 is the Jacobian from the parent square to the parameter cell.

The sum over cells is the assembly. Each cell e gives a local matrix [k] over the shape functions that are non-zero inside it, [k]\{\hat T_e\} = \{q\} + \{b\} = \{r\}, and its entries are added into the rows and columns of the corresponding global degrees of freedom, K_{IJ} \mathrel{+}= k_{ij}. Tap a cell in the physical view to see its Gauss points, [k] and where it lands in [K].

The loaded edges contribute to \{B\} through line integrals of the shape functions times the prescribed flux or traction, with Gauss points along the edge (gold arrows).

blocks.text:
[tool-form2d-s6] rz-tools form2d (heat conduction · Galerkin · Q4 Lagrange FEM) · 6 · The matrix system
Collecting the 25 component equations gives the discretized equation of the problem, a linear system for the 25 unknowns (which would be solved here; this tool stops before that):

[K]\{\hat T\} = \{Q\} + \{B\} = \{R\}, \qquad [K]\in\mathbb R^{25\times25}

[K] is symmetric, K_{IJ} = K_{JI}, because the weak form treats w_I and T^h alike, and sparse because each shape function overlaps few others: 130 non-zero entries of 20² (32.5 %), bandwidth 6.

The essential boundary condition has not been used yet; without it the system is singular. Methods:

Row–column condensation (partition). The unknowns on \Gamma_D are known (5 of them, subscript c); the rest are free (f). Partitioning the system and moving the known columns to the right-hand side:

\begin{bmatrix}[K_{ff}] & [K_{fc}]\\ [K_{cf}] & [K_{cc}]\end{bmatrix}\begin{Bmatrix}\{\hat T_f\}\\ \{\bar T_c\}\end{Bmatrix} = \begin{Bmatrix}\{R_f\}\\ \{R_c\}\end{Bmatrix} \qquad\Rightarrow\qquad [K_{ff}]\{\hat T_f\} = \{R_f\} - [K_{fc}]\{\bar T_c\}, \qquad 20\times20

With 5 values prescribed the system to be solved shrinks to 20 equations. The second row, [K_{cf}]\{\hat T_f\} + [K_{cc}]\{\bar T_c\} = \{R_c\}, gives the reactions (the boundary fluxes) afterwards. The method needs the boundary values to be nodal values, N_I(x_J,y_J) = \delta_{IJ} on \Gamma_D, or, for NURBS, that the boundary depends only on the boundary control values (true for an open knot vector; exact here because \bar T is constant).
